transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-06-30 10:00 PT
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Hannah Lee, Marco Diaz, Priya Nair (Redwood) — Aisha Khan, Ben Torres, Lina Park, Tom Reynolds (Kestrel)

Summary:
Quick sync to review last week's private pilot telemetry, discuss the unexpected routing spikes we saw Tuesday evening, decide whether to proceed with kernel 2.1.4 upgrade or rollback to 2.0.9 for the next canary, and assign clear owners for the burn-in and firewall validation.

[00:00] Hannah Lee: hey everyone, thanks for joining, uh, let's do quick intros then dive into the telemetry — marco, wanna kick off with the burn-in results?
[00:28] Marco Diaz: yeah, sure. so we ran the 48 hour low-batch and 24 hour high-batch tests, the main thing to call out is the spike pattern that lines up with the egress reshuffle — basically around 20:30 UTC we see 3x tail latency on p95, and the KV cache warmup was slower than expected, so payloads timed out.
[00:52] Aisha Khan: did you say egress reshuffle? that was our firewall rotating outbound IPs, we had a job that updated NAT twice an hour — we're still on a pretty aggressive refresh schedule for the NAT pool.
[01:12] Marco Diaz: right, so that churn causes some path changes; the runtime's smart routing falls back to the cross-region lane which adds 30-60ms. compounded when batching is high, tails blow up.
[01:35] Ben Torres: yes, we can slow the NAT rotation, but need to understand the exact port and fqdn expectations from Redwood. we already opened ports for grpc but maybe some telemetry endpoints were missed.
[01:50] Hannah Lee: good note. Priya — any compliance/security asks before we change egress timing?
[02:02] Priya Nair: just to record — Kestrel asked for audit logs retention details last week; we should confirm what we sent. also Tom from security is on, maybe he can double-check the KMS/HSM key flow for the private cluster.
[02:16] Tom Reynolds: yep — I need to validate that TLS termination for control plane calls is using mTLS and that keys remain customer‑managed in your proposed private control plane. also would like a short diagram of where logs are stored.
[02:34] Hannah Lee: understood, marco i'll add that to the doc pack.
[02:40] Marco Diaz: quick note — we observed a kernel upgrade (2.1.4) improved throughput by 8% on tailless profiles but increased tail latency in certain long-seq traces. quantization path also changed cache eviction slightly; i suspect the new attention kernel has a different prefetch pattern.
[03:05] Lina Park: hmm, so if we upgrade to 2.1.4 for canary burst, we risk worse tails during peak traffic — that was exactly what popped up on tuesday right?
[03:16] Marco Diaz: yeah that's the scenario. we can either roll forward with careful rate-limited canary and immediate fallback, or keep 2.0.9 and run workload‑specific microbenchmarks to see whether the throughput gain is worth the tail hit.
[03:35] Aisha Khan: what would be the rollback time if we do the canary and need to revert? our SRE runbook needs a ballpark.
[03:42] Hannah Lee: with our current plan, full rollback for the serving layer is about 12 minutes to revert kernels and rehydrate KV cache, plus another 10–15 minutes for client reconnects; we'll document steps so Lina can run it.
[04:05] Ben Torres: can you make sure we have a canary traffic split that stays below whatever threshold to keep SLA unaffected? say 5% traffic?
[04:17] Marco Diaz: yeah, canary at 1–3% to start, monitor tail, then bump to 5% if stable for 30 minutes. we also want a synthetic probe every 2 seconds to detect tail regression quickly.
[04:33] Hannah Lee: ok, burn-in results — marco, can you summarize the biggest red flags from the last run?
[04:40] Marco Diaz: red flags: 1) tail latency spikes caused by egress churn and fallback routing; 2) KV cache warmup slower under the new kernel for long sequences; 3) occasional TLS handshake retries on one node that correlated with CPU steal in the host.
[05:00] Lina Park: the TLS handshake retries — do you have IPs and timestamps? we can cross-ref our host telemetry.
[05:06] Marco Diaz: yes, i'll attach sample traces.
[05:10] Hannah Lee: and the good news?
[05:12] Marco Diaz: throughput improved overall, average latency dropped 6–8% for short requests under 128 tokens. so it's not all downside.
[05:20] Tom Reynolds: security note — when you mention KV cache, is any customer data persisted on Redwood-managed storage? we need to ensure PII is not cached or is encrypted.
[05:33] Marco Diaz: current pilot config uses ephemeral KV cache on host memory only, nothing persisted to disk. control plane logs are accessible to customers via the private control plane; we'll include the storage diagram.
[05:45] Hannah Lee: cool. next, firewall/egress checklist — Ben, what blockers do you expect to clear this week?
[05:54] Ben Torres: we need exact FQDNs for telemetry ingest and the health probe endpoints; also, if Redwood is going to use dynamic IPs for the canary, we'll need a signed certificate list or CIDR ranges. static IPs preferred.
[06:12] Hannah Lee: we can provide static egress ranges for the canary cluster and a list of hostnames. i'll put that in the follow-up email.
[06:20] Aisha Khan: about telemetry — are you providing a dashboard link or raw CSVs? we want to integrate with our internal observability (Splunk).
[06:30] Priya Nair: we'll share both: a Grafana link for Redwood telemetry plus a nightly CSV export for your Splunk ingestion.
[06:40] Lina Park: good. on the kernel decision — can we run a targeted microbenchmark that mirrors our production payloads? i.e., long sequences with high batch multipliers — to see if the cache warmup penalty is reproducible?
[06:55] Marco Diaz: yes, we can replay a subset of your live prompt traces using the workload harness. we'll need a redacted sample set and the expected token length distribution.
[07:10] Aisha Khan: i'll get 500 redacted traces over to marco by end of day tomorrow.
[07:16] Hannah Lee: perfect.
[07:20] [08:00] (brief cross-talk about calendar invites and timezone checking)
[08:12] Marco Diaz: one more technical point — the fallback routing logic currently prefers lowest-cost AZ path when it detects increased latency; that logic doesn't consider NAT churn and so it sometimes flips aggressively. a policy tweak to prefer stable path for the first 60s after a change would help.
[08:34] Ben Torres: could that policy be toggled per-customer during rollout?
[08:38] Marco Diaz: yes, we can set it as a per-account flag. we can turn on the conservative routing for Kestrel during the canary.
[08:46] Hannah Lee: ok, we'll enable conservative routing for the canary and monitor.
[08:52] Aisha Khan: question on billing — if we run extended burn-ins and extra canary monitoring, will that be part of the pilot commitment or billed separately?
[09:04] Hannah Lee: for the POC pilot we include up to two extended burn-ins; anything beyond that we can either absorb as part of the engineering support or add as an overage line item — we'll be explicit in the follow-up pricing note.
[09:20] Aisha Khan: ok please note that.
[09:25] [12:00] Marco Diaz: going through the telemetry graphs — here's the p95 overlay (i'm reading numbers) — Tuesday 20:24 UTC baseline p95 75ms, spike to 420ms for ~7 minutes, then settled back. traces show fallback to cross-region lane.
[09:52] Lina Park: do you have the specific node IDs for the instances that saw CPU steal?
[09:58] Marco Diaz: yeah, nodes redwood-nyc-12 and redwood-nyc-9.
[10:04] Ben Torres: i'll send our host-level logs for those timestamps, maybe it's a host maintenance job.
[10:12] Hannah Lee: thanks. action item: Marco will attach full trace IDs and node samples.
[10:18] Marco Diaz: noted.
[10:20] [18:00] Discussion about scheduling the canary: propose 2027-07-03 09:00 PT to do a controlled kernel rollout with rollback window of 30 minutes.
[10:39] Aisha Khan: that window works for our ops. lina will own the rollback and ben will manage the network changes.
[10:46] Hannah Lee: we'll prepare a step-by-step runbook and a one‑click rollback trigger in the console.
[10:54] Tom Reynolds: for compliance, we still need the SOC 2 evidence bundle and the log retention SLA — can you put those in the secure share?
[11:06] Priya Nair: yes, i'll upload the SOC 2 summary and retention table to the secure link and share by EOD 2027-07-01.
[11:14] Aisha Khan: perfect.
[11:20] [27:00] Quick parking-lot: discussion of continued quantization experiments; Kestrel asked for a small A/B on quantized model variant to test output parity. Marco to run a parity test on 200 samples.
[11:38] Marco Diaz: parity test for 200 traces — i'll run and report diffs, also include perplexity delta and token-level mismatches.
[11:45] Lina Park: please also note any hallucination differences; if quantization changes output, product may be sensitive.
[11:53] Marco Diaz: will do.
[12:00] [35:00] Pricing follow-up — Hannah: we'll send a short note showing pilot credits used and proposed additional burn-in support cost.
[12:10] Aisha Khan: can you separate the network-eng troubleshooting line item? we want transparency.
[12:18] Hannah Lee: yes, will line-item network engineering as a separate SKUs.
[12:24] [42:00] Wrap-up recap:
- Redwood actions: run 24h burn-in, attach traces, provide static egress IP list, toggle conservative routing flag, send kernel notes and quantization doc, upload SOC 2 + retention table.
- Kestrel actions: provide 500 redacted traces, confirm firewall/egress changes, prepare rollback runbook, own canary execution window.

[42:38] Hannah Lee: any final questions?
[42:44] Aisha Khan: no, thanks everyone — we'll aim to have the traces over to marco by tomorrow.
[42:50] Ben Torres: thanks, talk soon.
[42:54] Hannah Lee: thanks all, sending follow-up with action items and invites.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcription contains a few mis-heard words (KV cache sometimes rendered as "KV cash" in auto transcript), some speaker labels may be generic — please refer to action items and attachments for authoritative details.
